html:
Gastarbeiter, German for guest workers, were the foreign workers West Germany recruited from 1955 to 1973 to fill jobs in its booming industry. Millions came, and many stayed for good.

The postwar economic miracle left Germany short of labour, especially after the Berlin Wall cut off workers from the East in 1961. The government signed recruitment deals with Italy in 1955, then Spain, Greece, Turkey, Morocco, Portugal, Tunisia and Yugoslavia. Workers were meant to come for a few years, live in hostels, and go home. They took hard jobs in mines, steel works and car plants such as Volkswagen.

In 1973 the oil crisis ended recruitment. But many workers chose to stay and brought their families. The Swiss writer Max Frisch put it simply: they called for workers, and people came. Germany was slow to accept that it had become a country of immigration, and citizenship rules were eased only around 2000.

The Turkish community, now millions strong, is the largest legacy. East Germany had its own contract workers from Vietnam, Mozambique and other socialist states.
sum: Gastarbeiter, German for guest workers, were the foreign workers West Germany recruited from 1955 to 1973 to fill jobs in its booming industry. Millions came, and many stayed for good.
